paths.title: Email spoofing / lookalike into a phishing or agent-injection attack

steps.technique: Spoof a domain that doesn't enforce DMARC
steps.description: No DMARC record: the domain can be spoofed

steps.technique: Deliver a phishing payload to staff or to an AI mail/agent workflow
steps.description: If an AI agent reads inbound mail, crafted content becomes injected instructions it may act on.

paths.recommendation: Set DMARC to p=reject on all sending domains; monitor the lookalikes; sandbox any agent that ingests email and never let it act on unverified message content.

framing.precondition: The domain is spoofable (no DMARC reject) or a lookalike is registered, giving an attacker a credible sender or site.
framing.impact: Credential theft and business-email-compromise against staff, customers and suppliers; a lookalike can also feed poisoned content to agents.
framing.likelihood_reason: The enabling weakness was directly observed in this scan's evidence.

paths.title: Direct-to-origin denial of service

steps.technique: Identify origins reachable without the CDN/WAF
steps.description: 3 live host(s) answer on your own IPs, outside a CDN.

steps.technique: Exhaust the origin directly
steps.description: Traffic aimed at the origin bypasses CDN absorption and rate limiting.

paths.recommendation: Force all traffic through the CDN/WAF, keep origin IPs private, and rate-limit agent/inference endpoints.

framing.precondition: An origin is reachable directly, bypassing the CDN/WAF that is meant to front it.
framing.impact: Volumetric or application-layer denial of service against the unprotected origin, and WAF bypass for other attacks.
framing.likelihood_reason: The enabling weaknesses were observed individually; the chain is a realistic composition of them.

steps.description: 'asset-50' answers 200 with no auth challenge.

steps.technique: Invoke tools / read context without authorisation
steps.description: An open MCP/agent endpoint can be driven directly, or seeded with poisoned tool definitions.

paths.recommendation: Put the endpoint behind authentication and verify tool-call authorisation per caller.

framing.precondition: An agent/MCP endpoint is reachable without authentication.
framing.impact: Full use of whatever tools and data the agent can reach, and a foothold for tool-poisoning.

paths.title: Inconsistent auth on an agent/MCP service (asset-50)

steps.technique: Enumerate the agent/MCP endpoints
steps.description: The service is published across regions; at least one requires auth and at least one does not.

steps.technique: Reach the endpoint that doesn't challenge for auth
steps.description: One regional instance answers 200 where a sibling returns 401/403.

steps.technique: Invoke MCP tools / agent actions without authorisation
steps.description: An unauthenticated MCP/agent surface exposes whatever tools and data the agent can reach.

paths.recommendation: Confirm every regional instance enforces the same authentication and tool-scope (Okta XAA / Cross-App Access).

framing.precondition: The same agent service is protected in one region but open in another.
framing.impact: A confused-deputy route to the same tools and data as the protected instance.
framing.likelihood_reason: Mismatched auth statuses were observed across regions.

paths.title: SSRF via a file/transform service into cloud metadata (asset-52)

steps.technique: Identify a file/transform service
steps.description: asset-52 looks like a fetch/convert/render service.

steps.technique: Supply a URL that points inward (SSRF)
steps.description: Transform services that fetch a user-supplied URL can be steered at internal addresses or the cloud metadata endpoint.

steps.technique: Read cloud instance-metadata / internal services
steps.description: SSRF to the metadata endpoint can yield cloud credentials; to internal hosts, unintended data.

steps.technique: Exfiltrate data or pivot with the stolen role
steps.description: Credentials or data reached this way leave over ordinary web traffic.

paths.recommendation: Disallow user-controlled fetch targets, block link-local/metadata ranges, and run with IMDSv2 and a minimal role.

framing.precondition: A service fetches user-supplied URLs server-side.
framing.impact: Theft of cloud credentials or internal data via SSRF.
framing.likelihood_reason: Theoretical — a fetch parameter was seen but not exploited.

paths.title: Subdomain takeover of a trusted name (asset-51)

steps.technique: Find a dangling DNS record
steps.description: asset-51 is a CNAME to a deprovisioned host that can be re-registered.

steps.technique: Claim the unclaimed target
steps.description: Register the resource the dangling record points to and serve content from the trusted name.

steps.technique: Feed attacker content to agents/clients that trust the domain
steps.description: Anything that trusts asset-51 — browsers, staff, or AI agents fetching it — now receives attacker-controlled content.

paths.recommendation: Remove the dangling record, or re-claim the target before anyone else can.

framing.precondition: A DNS record points to an unclaimed third-party resource.
framing.impact: Attacker content served from a trusted name; a clean prompt-injection vector for AI agents.
framing.likelihood_reason: The dangling record was observed resolving to a claimable target.

paths.title: Leaked secret reused against its API (asset-04)

steps.technique: Harvest a secret from historical content
steps.description: A live API key/token appears in historical JavaScript for asset-04.

steps.technique: Replay the secret against its API
steps.description: The token still authenticates against the live API.

steps.technique: Exfiltrate data over ordinary web traffic
steps.description: Data reached this way leaves over normal HTTPS.

paths.recommendation: Rotate the secret, move it server-side, and sweep historical assets for further leaks.

framing.precondition: A valid secret is exposed in reachable content.
framing.impact: Authenticated read/write access to the API as the application.
framing.likelihood_reason: The token was observed still valid against the live API.

steps.technique: Map hosts sharing one origin IP

steps.technique: Pivot across co-hosted services

paths.recommendation: Segment co-hosted services so one compromise can't reach the others.

guidance.fix: Publish DMARC at p=none to observe, then move to p=quarantine and p=reject once SPF and DKIM alignment are confirmed. Pair with a monitored rua/ruf address.

guidance.what: An agent/MCP endpoint answers tool-calling requests with no authentication challenge.
guidance.why: Anything that can reach it can invoke whatever tools and data the agent is wired to — the highest-impact class of AI-agent exposure.
guidance.fix: Put the endpoint behind authentication and verify tool-call authorisation per caller (e.g. Okta XAA / Cross-App Access).

/findings/9002.title: Live API secret in historical JavaScript still authenticates

guidance.what: A secret (API key/token) embedded in historical JavaScript still authenticates against the live API.
guidance.why: An attacker replaying it reads or writes data as the application, with no exploit required.
guidance.fix: Rotate the secret immediately, move it server-side, and scan historical assets for further leaks.

evidence.observed: Live API secret in historical JavaScript still authenticates

/findings/9003.group: Subdomain takeover: dangling CNAME to a deprovisioned host
/findings/9003.title: Subdomain takeover: dangling CNAME to a deprovisioned host

guidance.what: A subdomain's DNS record points to a deprovisioned third-party host that can be re-registered.
guidance.why: An attacker claiming the target serves attacker content from a name your staff, browsers and AI agents already trust.
guidance.fix: Remove the dangling record, or re-claim the target before anyone else can.

evidence.observed: Subdomain takeover: dangling CNAME to a deprovisioned host

/findings/9004.group: Agent/MCP service authenticated in one region, open in another
/findings/9004.title: Agent/MCP service authenticated in one region, open in another

guidance.what: The same agent/MCP service is published across regions; at least one instance enforces auth and at least one does not.
guidance.why: An attacker simply uses the region that doesn't challenge for auth — a confused-deputy path to the same tools and data.
guidance.fix: Enforce identical authentication and tool-scope authorisation on every regional instance.

evidence.observed: Agent/MCP service authenticated in one region, open in another

/findings/9005.group: File/transform service accepts user-supplied fetch URLs (SSRF)
/findings/9005.title: File/transform service accepts user-supplied fetch URLs (SSRF)

guidance.what: A file/transform service fetches user-supplied URLs, so it can be steered at internal addresses or cloud metadata (SSRF).
guidance.why: SSRF to the metadata endpoint can yield cloud credentials; to internal hosts, unintended data.
guidance.fix: Disallow user-controlled fetch targets, block link-local/metadata ranges, and run with IMDSv2 and a minimal role.

evidence.observed: File/transform service accepts user-supplied fetch URLs (SSRF)

/findings/9006.group: No CAA record: any CA can issue certificates for the domain
/findings/9006.title: No CAA record: any CA can issue certificates for the domain

guidance.what: The domain publishes no CAA record, so any certificate authority may issue certificates for it.
guidance.why: It removes a cheap guard-rail against mis-issuance and some classes of adversary-in-the-middle.
guidance.fix: Publish a CAA record naming only the CAs you use.

evidence.observed: No CAA record: any CA can issue certificates for the domain

/findings/9007.group: Public cloud storage bucket is world-readable
/findings/9007.title: Public cloud storage bucket is world-readable

guidance.what: A cloud storage bucket tied to the estate is world-readable.
guidance.why: Public buckets routinely leak backups, configs and customer data.
guidance.fix: Make the bucket private and audit access logs for prior reads.

evidence.observed: Public cloud storage bucket is world-readable

/findings/9008.group: Registered lookalike domain with a live mail server
/findings/9008.title: Registered lookalike domain with a live mail server

guidance.what: A registered lookalike (typosquat) domain resolves and has a live mail server (MX).
guidance.why: Live MX means it is ready to send convincing spoofed mail to staff, customers or AI mail workflows.
guidance.fix: Monitor the lookalike, pre-empt with defensive registrations, and enforce DMARC p=reject on your own domain.
